records.basis: Kepler chapter LVIII and Russell pp. 2–3 support the Mars-only ellipse with the Sun at one focus; Lower is a named independent reader, not evidence of universal adoption.

The Principia Book III pp. 405–412 states the qualified synthesis. The unsigned 1688 review, independently attributed to Locke, summarizes mutual astronomical forces and all-body/particle gravity; it does not prove Locke independently checked the proofs.
The 1609 title leaf and chapter LVIII p. 285 state the elliptical result; the next chapter names Mars. Russell p. 3 limits the 1609 formulation to Mars.

Stevens pp. 120–124 transcribes Lower reading and approving the elliptical theory while reporting difficulty and disagreement over magnetic causes. Chapman explains the 1610/1611 ambiguity; the manuscript was not inspected.
The retained 1687 Latin pages include Propositions II and IV–VII and Corollary 2 on equal particles; their presence does not establish independent verification of the complete mathematical proof.

The 1944 transcription of the 1690 Addition pp. 471–472 rejects the attraction among small parts while allowing celestial centripetal tendency; this is critical recognition, not acceptance of all-particle gravity.

Whiston 1696 Book I pp. 2–5 states the mutual-attraction and inverse-square premises, with uncertainty over physical cause; Ducheyne and van Besouw link his account to Newton without endorsing its theological narrative.

Original 1688 printing p. 371 / PDF p. 386 states mutual celestial-body gravitation, gravity in all bodies proportional to matter and inverse-square dependence for equal particles. Iliffe attributes the unsigned review to Locke. A summary does not prove independent verification or full acceptance.

The original title leaf is dated 1688 and the review heading and substance appear at printed pp. 363 and 371 / PDF pp. 378 and 386. This printing differs in pagination from another commonly cited copy.
